extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and mathematical researchers (analysis, differential equations, topology, algebra, geometry)
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of open mathematical research problems (Hilbert's problems) spanning differential equations, algebraic forms, geometry of space, function theory, and the calculus of variations, with explanatory context and suggested methods. Intended as an agenda for future mathematical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum number and position of Poincaré boundary cycles for first-order rational differential equations
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the maximum number and the possible positions of Poincaré's boundary cycles (limit cycles) for a first-order differential equation of the form dy/dx = Y/X, where X and Y are rational integral functions of degree n in x and y (written homogeneously: X(y dz/dt − z dy/dt) + Y(z dx/dt − x dz/dt) + Z(x dy/dt − y dx/dt) = 0 with X,Y,Z homogeneous of degree n)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert suggests attacking this by the method of continuous variation of coefficients and notes the topological significance for families of curves defined by differential equations. The homogeneous formulation and the relation to topology of curve families are emphasized as useful perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of definite forms by squares (and quotients of sums of squares)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a rational integral form (in any number of variables with real coefficients) that never becomes negative for real variable values (a definite form), can every such definite form be expressed as a quotient of sums of squares of forms? (Hilbert remarks he has answered this affirmatively for ternary forms.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes: the square of any form is definite, sums and products preserve definiteness, and quotients may be definite if integral. An additional desirable refinement is to know whether the coefficients in such representations can be taken from the same field of rationality as the coefficients of the original form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationality of coefficients in sums-of-squares representations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a definite form is represented as a quotient of sums of squares of forms, can the coefficients of the forms used in the representation always be chosen from the same realm of rationality as the coefficients of the represented form?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert highlights this as an important refinement relevant to geometrical constructions; he earlier established positive results for ternary forms but raises this as a general question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finiteness of essentially different motion groups with fundamental regions in n-dimensional Euclidean space
rubrics_metrics.description: Is there in n-dimensional Euclidean space only a finite number of essentially different kinds of groups of motions that admit a fundamental region?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context: analogous facts are known for elliptic and hyperbolic planes/space (finite kinds in elliptic, infinite in hyperbolic, intermediate behavior in Euclidean 2D/3D). Jordan's theorem gives finiteness for elliptic space; Fricke & Klein studied hyperbolic; Fedorov, Schoenflies, and Rohn proved finiteness results in 3D Euclidean space. Hilbert notes the n-dimensional Euclidean generalization seems difficult and desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of polyhedra that tile space but are not fundamental regions of motion groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Do there exist polyhedra which do not appear as fundamental regions of groups of motions, but nevertheless by juxtaposition of congruent copies can produce a complete filling (tiling) of all space?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is posed as a question related to groups of motions and fundamental regions; Hilbert flags it as important and relates it to the previous problem about motion groups with fundamental regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Densest packing of equal solids in space (sphere/tetrahedron packing)
rubrics_metrics.description: How can one arrange most densely in space an infinite number of equal solids of given form (e.g., spheres of given radii or regular tetrahedra with given edges or in prescribed position) so that the ratio of filled to unfilled space is as large as possible?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert frames this as a question relevant to number theory and possibly to physics and chemistry — essentially the densest-packing (Kepler) problem. He invites investigation of optimal fit and densest arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyticity of solutions to regular variational problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Do solutions of 'regular' problems in the calculus of variations necessarily have to be analytic functions of the independent variables? (Regular problems are those whose integrand F(p,q,z;x,y) is analytic and satisfies the condition F_{pp} F_{qq} - (F_{pq})^2 > 0 for all relevant arguments.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert explains that many PDEs (potential equation, certain linear equations, minimal surface equation, and others) have only analytic solutions; he asks whether every Lagrangian PDE arising from a regular variation problem admits only analytic integrals. He raises subtleties when boundary values are only continuous (e.g., Dirichlet problem) and notes examples: some surfaces of constant negative Gaussian curvature are C^∞ but not analytic, whereas surfaces of positive constant curvature are probably analytic. The question is to determine when regular variational problems force analyticity of solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: General problem of boundary values (existence under prescribed boundary conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: For partial differential equations, under what conditions do solutions exist when values (or differential relations) are prescribed on the boundary of the region? Can existence theorems (beyond potential theory) be proved by a general principle indicated by Dirichlet's principle?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert notes that methods of Schwarz, Neumann, and Poincaré solve the potential equation but do not extend directly to cases prescribing differential coefficients on the boundary, nor to problems for least-area surfaces or surfaces of constant positive curvature with given boundary curves. He conjectures a general principle (in the spirit of Dirichlet's principle) might prove existence of solutions for regular variation problems given suitable assumptions about boundary data (e.g., continuity and some derivatives), perhaps with generalized notions of solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of linear differential equations with a prescribed monodromic (monodromy) group (Fuchsian class)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that for given singular points and a prescribed monodromic (monodromy) group there exists a linear differential equation of the Fuchsian class whose solutions (n functions) are regular except at the prescribed singular points and undergo the prescribed linear substitutions when analytically continued around those points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert remarks that this existence is plausible by counting constants, but rigorous proofs were known only in special cases (e.g., when characteristic roots of the given substitutions have absolute value 1); L. Schlesinger treated that special case using Poincaré's theory of Fuchsian zeta-functions. Hilbert calls for a completely general method to resolve the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformization of analytic relations by automorphic functions (and generalization to several variables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend Poincaré's theorem (that any algebraic relation between two variables can be reduced to uniformity by automorphic functions of one variable) to arbitrary analytic (non-algebraic) relations between two variables, and further to relations among three or more complex variables. In particular, can the resolving functions be chosen so that as the new variable traverses the regular domain all regular points of the given analytic field are represented (i.e., avoid the presence of additional discrete exceptional points)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert notes Poincaré's successes and methods, but also mentions that Poincaré's constructions may leave additional exceptional points accessible only as limiting values of the new variable. He calls for elucidation of this difficulty and generalization to higher numbers of variables, referencing Picard's investigations as useful preliminary work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Further development of methods of the calculus of variations (Weierstrass, Jacobi, multi-variable extensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop and modernize methods in the calculus of variations: sharpen Weierstrass's theory, clarify Jacobi's condition and its necessity/sufficiency (in conjunction with Weierstrass's E > 0), extend polar-process methods, and generalize results to multiple integrals, multiple functions, and higher-dimensional variational problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert praises recent work (e.g., A. Kneser's modern treatment) and explains how the polar process applied to Euler–Lagrange equations leads to Weierstrass' expression E and to Jacobi's condition; he outlines analogous constructions for double and multiple integrals, the associated first-order PDEs (characteristics), and gives formulae (Weierstrass expression E, variational equalities) that play the same role in higher dimensions. He points to Kneser's modified approach using simple families of integral curves and the construction of characteristic solutions of generalized Jacobi–Hamilton equations. The problem is both to refine theory (textbooks, methods) and to extend existence/optimality criteria.
